q: In what style is the 11th-century Baptistery of Florence?
n: The Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence (11th–12th c.) is a key work of Florentine Romanesque, with geometric green-and-white marble cladding. Source: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore (official site).

q: Which cathedral forms a famous group with its baptistery, campanile and Camposanto?
n: Pisa Cathedral forms the famous Piazza dei Miracoli group with the Baptistery, the Leaning Tower and the Camposanto. Source: UNESCO (Piazza del Duomo, Pisa).

q: Which is often called the smallest cathedral in the world?
n: The 9th-century Church of the Holy Cross at Nin, Croatia, is often called the smallest cathedral in the world. Source: Croatian National Tourist Board; Nin town tourist office.

q: A wagon vault is based on the principle of the:
n: A wagon (barrel) vault is an arch extended in depth. It works on the arch principle, in compression, and pushes outward on its walls. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What happens to an arch when it is extruded along its axis?
n: An arch extruded along its axis forms a barrel (tunnel) vault. A dome is an arch rotated about its vertical axis. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Schodek, Structures.

q: A barrel or wagon vault is also called a:
n: A barrel or wagon vault is also called a tunnel vault. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What resisted the outward thrust of Romanesque barrel vaults?
n: The outward thrust of Romanesque barrel vaults was resisted by thick masonry walls, helped by flat buttresses. Flying buttresses came with Gothic. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Why were Romanesque interiors dim?
n: Romanesque interiors were dim because the thick, load-bearing walls allowed only small, deeply set windows. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Romanesque architecture.

q: What is the bishop's throne in a cathedral called?
n: The cathedra is the bishop's throne. A cathedral is the church that holds it. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What raised stand was used for reading the Gospel and Epistles in early churches?
n: The ambo is a raised stand or platform in early Christian churches from which the Gospel and Epistles were read. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher.

q: What is the entrance porch at the west end of an Early Christian or Byzantine church?
n: The narthex is the entrance porch or vestibule at the west end of an Early Christian or Byzantine church, used by catechumens and penitents. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is the typical plan of Early Christian churches?
n: Early Christian churches followed the basilican plan, adapted from the Roman basilica: a nave with aisles, clerestory and apse, as at Old St. Peter's. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which style is plain outside but rich inside?
n: Byzantine churches are typically plain brick outside but richly finished inside with marble revetment and gold mosaics, as at Ravenna and Hagia Sophia. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Byzantine architecture.

q: Hagia Sophia is an example of which style?
n: Hagia Sophia (532–537) is the masterpiece of Byzantine architecture. Source: UNESCO (Historic Areas of Istanbul).

q: What is true about a merlon in medieval architecture?
n: A merlon is the solid upstanding part of a crenellated parapet, between the gaps (crenels). Many merlons were pierced with narrow arrow slits so archers could shoot while protected. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Encyclopaedia Britannica, battlement.

q: Which term goes with the crenellations of medieval castles?
n: Crenellations are made of alternating merlons and gaps called crenels or embrasures. A bartizan is a corner turret. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: What is the defining structural feature of Byzantine churches?
n: The defining structural feature of Byzantine churches is a central dome on pendentives. Rib vaults and flying buttresses are Gothic. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which post-colonial phase structure features a dome and Palladian style?
n: The US Capitol (from 1793, dome 1855–66) is a Neoclassical, Palladian-influenced building crowned by a great cast-iron dome, from the post-colonial Federal period. Source: Architect of the Capitol (official site).

q: Who designed Hagia Sophia?
o: Isidore of Meant and Isidore of Taft
Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles
Isidore of Melenia and Anthemius of Tralles
Isidore of Tran and Anthemius of Troll
n: Hagia Sophia was designed by Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles for Emperor Justinian. Source: UNESCO (Historic Areas of Istanbul); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What was Hagia Sophia from 1453 to 1931?
n: After the Ottoman conquest of 1453 Hagia Sophia was converted into a mosque. It served as one until it was made a museum (decree 1934, opened 1935). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hagia Sophia.

q: What is the most common material used in the construction of the Hagia Sophia?
n: Hagia Sophia is built mainly of brick laid in thick mortar, with ashlar stone for the main piers and marble revetment inside. Of the choices, ashlar bricks best fits this masonry construction. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hagia Sophia; Mainstone, Hagia Sophia.

q: What is Hagia Sophia used as today?
n: In July 2020 Hagia Sophia was reconverted from a museum into a mosque, which it remains today. It is still open to visitors outside prayer times. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hagia Sophia; UNESCO statement (2020).

q: What feature of Hagia Sophia lets light into the dome so it seems to float?
o: A ring of windows at the dome's base
n: Hagia Sophia's dome rests on a ring of 40 closely spaced windows at its base. The band of light breaks the visual support, so the dome seems to float, as Procopius described. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hagia Sophia; Mainstone, Hagia Sophia.

q: Figure 08-B: What is the architectural style of Figure B?
n: Figure B, Pisa Cathedral with its campanile, is Pisan Romanesque: round arches and tiers of arcaded galleries in striped marble. Source: UNESCO (Piazza del Duomo, Pisa).

q: Figure 08-B: What is the architectural style of Figure C?
n: Figure C, Milan Cathedral (begun 1386), is Gothic, with pinnacles, pointed tracery and flying buttresses. Source: Veneranda Fabbrica del Duomo di Milano; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Figure 08-B: What is the architectural style of Figure D?
n: Figure D, Hagia Sophia, is the defining Byzantine church, with a great dome on pendentives. Source: UNESCO (Historic Areas of Istanbul).

q: Figure 08-B: What is the architectural style of Figure E?
n: Figure E, the Obradoiro facade of Santiago de Compostela Cathedral (1738–50, by Fernando de Casas Novoa), is Spanish Baroque. Source: UNESCO (Santiago de Compostela, Old Town).

q: What is the name of Figure A, an example of a Byzantine church?
n: Figure A, Hagia Sophia in Istanbul (532–537), is the archetypal Byzantine church. Source: UNESCO (Historic Areas of Istanbul).

q: What is the name of Figure B, an example of a Renaissance church?
n: Figure B is St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, the great Renaissance church of Bramante, Michelangelo and Maderno. Source: UNESCO (Vatican City); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is the name of Figure C, an example of a Renaissance chapel?
n: Figure C is Bramante's Tempietto at San Pietro in Montorio, Rome (about 1502), a small circular High Renaissance chapel. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Donato Bramante.

q: What is the name of Figure D, an example of a Renaissance building?
n: Figure D is Palladio's Villa Capra "La Rotonda" near Vicenza (begun about 1567), a centrally planned Renaissance villa. Source: UNESCO (City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto).

q: What is the name of Figure E, an example of a Gothic church?
n: Figure E is Reims Cathedral, a High Gothic church, the coronation site of French kings. Source: UNESCO (Reims Cathedral).

q: Key factor of space planning.
n: Ergonomics, fitting spaces and furniture to human dimensions and movement, is the key factor of space planning. Layout and clearances start from how people use the space. Source: Panero & Zelnik, Human Dimension & Interior Space; Time-Saver Standards for Interior Design.
